prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks based on magic-wavelength trapping, which brought frequency measurement to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I have moved my preferred configuration from B006 to B024. The reason is the test I applied myself in round 1: which result has taught us something that was tested hard and has stayed put. The magic-wavelength lattice is a single idea, a trapping wavelength at which the differential light shift of the clock transition vanishes while many atoms are held in the Lamb-Dicke regime, free of Doppler and recoil shifts. It was then realized in strontium and ytterbium to roughly 10^-18, and independent laboratories reproduce it and compare clocks against each other. That is a physics result with a sharp, checkable outcome, and the credit maps onto two people: Katori for the concept and Ye for the record performance and the many-body, spin-polarized clock regime. The discovery content Pearce asked about is real to me. Millimetre-scale gravitational redshift resolved in a single sample, bounds on drifts of constants and the many-body systematics of a degenerate Fermi gas are physics results, and a clock this good is also a statistical-mechanics object in its own right. The distinction from 2005 and 2012 can be written into the citation: the comb supplied a frequency ruler and the ion prize recognized control of one quantum system, whereas this prize is for interrogating many neutral atoms at once in a state-insensitive trap.
statement.case_against: The reservations that kept B024 seventh on my opening list are narrowed but not gone. A third clock-related prize invites the charge of incrementalism on ground already honoured in 2005 and 2012, and the citation must carry the distinction explicitly and not leave it to the reader. The redefinition of the second has not happened, and I think it is irrelevant to the discovery but it is a fair line for a sceptic. The pair omits Lemonde, Sterr, Hollberg and the ion-clock leaders, and I cannot resolve from the shortlist alone whether Ye co-invented or realized, though a two-name prize with a citation that says invention and realization is defensible either way. Against my former choice: I have to answer Johansson and Pearce directly, namely that the quantitative evidence for Toner-Tu exponents is partial and the committee cannot assume the other members will weigh it more favourably than I do. B006 also has no second supporter, and the cutoff against Marchetti, Cates, Simha and Chate remains arbitrary. I do not treat that as a verdict on active matter, only as a judgment about this year's maturity and credit.

responses.point: Johansson asked whether I see experimental evidence for the Toner-Tu exponents beyond qualitative agreement, and argued that a Nobel Prize should rest on a result tested hard.
responses.response: The honest answer is limited evidence. Giant number fluctuations, long-range order in two dimensions and the generic existence of a collective-motion transition are well documented in simulations, vibrated granular layers and bacterial and colloidal systems. Numerical estimates of the Toner-Tu exponents are in rough agreement with the one-loop prediction in simulations but lack the precision that comparisons across laboratories give for clocks, and experiments cannot reach the asymptotic scaling regime cleanly. I take his standard as correct and it has moved me. I also agree with his drafting suggestion: tie the citation to the magic-wavelength lattice and its realization, and do not widen it to the clock community. I would additionally ask him to confirm that the many-body systematic budget he queried for Ye is settled at the level the headline uncertainty implies, because that decides whether Ye is credited as a physicist or only as the owner of the best system.

responses.point: Pearce asked whether I regard the clock result as a measurement advance without discovery content, or whether tests of constants and relativistic redshift change that view.
responses.response: They change it. I ranked B024 seventh mainly out of field distance, and I now regard the discovery content as real: resolving the gravitational redshift across a millimetre-scale atomic sample, limiting drifts of constants and operating a degenerate Fermi gas as a clock where interaction shifts enter the systematic budget are physics outcomes, not instrument polish. I also agree with Pearce that the concern about metrology as an instrument achievement is the strongest against B024 and the committee should answer it openly. My answer is that the invention made a measurement possible that no earlier scheme delivered, which is the same standard we apply to other instrument-type prizes. I do share his worry about the ion-clock and SYRTE and PTB contributions, and I would handle it in the citation wording and the committee's public explanation, not by enlarging the prize beyond three names.

responses.point: Olsson asked that the chronology of the first demonstration be checked before the citation is fixed and accepted that Ye's role may be better described as realization than as co-invention.
responses.response: I accept her framing and propose we adopt it. The citation I put forward says invention and realization, and that wording is robust whichever way the chronology comes out: Katori is credited for the concept and for the first realizations, Ye for the record accuracy and the many-body programme. I also take her point that the comb and ion prizes are enabling prior art, not duplicates, and I think a sentence in the citation naming many atoms interrogated at a magic wavelength meets it. I would only stress that the chronology check is the Committee's work and cannot be settled from my profile or from the shortlist record, so I regard it as a precondition to be confirmed, not as something I have verified.

responses.point: Danielsson holds that B003 is an original discovery, that prediction followed by experiment makes it the cleanest story on the list, and that unsettled pairing should not block a prize for the phases themselves.
responses.response: I take his precedent argument seriously, since high-temperature superconductors were rewarded before the mechanism was known, and the 2011 prediction of flat bands is on much firmer ground than the interpretation of the experiments. That is why B003 is in my alternatives and not further down. What I still cannot get round is the credit: the three-person limit leaves out Cao and the early confirming groups, and the dispute about whether Bistritzer or Jarillo-Herrero's group leader is the right second and third name has not been argued out. Eriksson's remark that the three-name rule forces that cost is right, but it is an argument for waiting for a clearer assignment, not for accepting it now. If the Committee still prefers B003 I would want the citation restricted to flat bands and correlated states and silent on pairing.

uncertainties: Whether the citation can state the distinction from the 2005 comb and 2012 single-ion prizes crisply enough to answer the incrementalism charge.
Whether Lemonde, Sterr, Hollberg and the ion-clock leaders have a claim strong enough to change the credited pair, and whether Ye is credited for co-invention or for realization.
Whether the pending redefinition of the second should be awaited, which I regard as irrelevant to the discovery but not as an unreasonable view.

Whether B003 will look mature once the superconducting mechanism and the credit question settle, and whether B006 will in time acquire quantitative tests of the Toner-Tu exponents and a cleaner three-name cutoff.
statement.conflict_note: No specific personal or institutional conflict is apparent from the profile. My field is statistical physics of complex systems and my earlier first choice B006 was scientifically close to it, but I have no documented tie to Toner, Ramaswamy or Vicsek, nor to Katori, Ye or the other named candidates, and I do not regard field proximity to B006 as bearing on B024. I note the disclosures of Kroll (Hall laboratory stay), Lindroth and Olsson (Japanese university ties) on B024 and would defer to the Chair on any ruling; none appears to me to require recusal.
